claims.text: Introducing a secondary phase or precipitates into single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy-alloy derivatives can enhance coercivity.
A secondary phase or precipitates can create pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Domain-wall pinning caused by the introduced secondary phase can enhance coercivity.
Introducing a secondary phase or precipitates can modify the alloy microstructure.
The modified microstructure reduces magnetic anisotropy.
Reducing magnetic anisotropy contributes to enhanced coercivity.
The intervention could raise coercivity above 100 Oe.
Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its relevant derivatives have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe.
The proposed comparison is between otherwise matched samples with and without an introduced secondary phase or precipitates.
Failure to obtain a significant coercivity increase, exemplified by failure to exceed 100 Oe in multiple samples, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention deliberately introduces a secondary phase or precipitates, while the stated conditions and boundary require a single-phase fcc structure. It is not clarified whether single-phase fcc applies only before intervention or must remain true afterward.
Reduced magnetic anisotropy is presented as a route to increased coercivity, but this direction is mechanistically questionable and is not reconciled with the claimed coercivity enhancement.
